questions.q: The Prophet told his persecuted Companions to go to Abyssinia, “where there is a king under whose rule people are safe.” What does the article draw from this?
options: Believers should live only under rulers of their own faith
Not quite. The article says: Security and social peace are to be valued under any just ruler, whatever his faith – and whatever destroys them is rejected.
Security and social peace are to be valued under any just ruler, whatever his faith – and whatever destroys them is rejected
Yes. The article calls terrorism forbidden from every point of view.
Safety matters less than political power
Not quite. The article says: Security and social peace are to be valued under any just ruler, whatever his faith – and whatever destroys them is rejected.
Migration is always better than staying
Not quite. The article says: Security and social peace are to be valued under any just ruler, whatever his faith – and whatever destroys them is rejected.
questions.rationale: “Islam rejects anything that destroys social peace, terrorises populace, or takes innocent lives… establishing a peaceful society is praiseworthy, even if its guardian is a sovereign following another faith.”

questions.q: “Counterfeit gold is only considered gold until it has been put to the test of the touchstone.” What is the touchstone in the article’s comparison?
options: The Day of Reckoning, when pretence falls away and each person appears as he truly is
Right. Until then, words can disguise deeds.
The passage of a few years
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Reckoning, when pretence falls away and each person appears as he truly is.
Public opinion
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Reckoning, when pretence falls away and each person appears as he truly is.
A court of law
Not quite. The article says: The Day of Reckoning, when pretence falls away and each person appears as he truly is.
questions.rationale: “It can only prevail until the Day of Reckoning comes to pass, when God’s truth will eliminate all falsehood.”

questions.q: Which failing of outwardly religious people does the article describe?
options: Praying too briefly
Not quite. The article says: Keeping the rituals while still lying, being proud and unjust – treating religion as talk, not practice.
Asking too many questions
Not quite. The article says: Keeping the rituals while still lying, being proud and unjust – treating religion as talk, not practice.
Giving too much in charity
Not quite. The article says: Keeping the rituals while still lying, being proud and unjust – treating religion as talk, not practice.
Keeping the rituals while still lying, being proud and unjust – treating religion as talk, not practice
Yes. Ritual made to look like the real thing.
questions.rationale: “When they fast, they assiduously abstain from food and drink, but they do not bother to refrain from lying, deceit, and injustice.”

questions.q: What does the article say later generations inherited from the early believers, and what did they miss?
options: The memory of past greatness, without the humility that produced it
Well read. “God elevates the humble.”
Their wealth, without their learning
Not quite. The article says: The memory of past greatness, without the humility that produced it.
Their humility, without their history
Not quite. The article says: The memory of past greatness, without the humility that produced it.
Nothing at all
Not quite. The article says: The memory of past greatness, without the humility that produced it.
questions.rationale: “They have inherited from them not their humility, but only the recollection of the great heights to which their remote ancestors rose.”

questions.q: A warship’s advanced computer mistook a passenger plane for a fighter. What argument does the article build from such errors?
options: Technology will soon be perfect
Not quite. The article says: Man-made systems fail even under close watch, so the faultless working of the vast universe points to intelligent design.
The universe is full of similar errors
Not quite. The article says: Man-made systems fail even under close watch, so the faultless working of the vast universe points to intelligent design.
Computers should not be used at sea
Not quite. The article says: Man-made systems fail even under close watch, so the faultless working of the vast universe points to intelligent design.
Man-made systems fail even under close watch, so the faultless working of the vast universe points to intelligent design
Correct. A mere machine would go wrong.
questions.rationale: “If such failures can occur in a highly monitored environment, it seems even more unlikely that the vast, precise universe could come into existence and operate on its own.”

questions.q: A journalist said of Africa that “God is in the air over there.” How does the article explain such a feeling?
options: Nature untouched by man is God’s direct handiwork, and so the best setting for remembering Him
Yes. City life absorbs us in man-made things.
Journalists are easily impressed
Not quite. The article says: Nature untouched by man is God’s direct handiwork, and so the best setting for remembering Him.
Africa is nearer to heaven
Not quite. The article says: Nature untouched by man is God’s direct handiwork, and so the best setting for remembering Him.
Cities have no beauty at all
Not quite. The article says: Nature untouched by man is God’s direct handiwork, and so the best setting for remembering Him.
questions.rationale: “Nature is the direct handiwork of God. That’s why in the natural world, it’s as if God becomes visible.”

questions.q: A broken stone in the Red Fort museum carries a prayer that an emperor’s kingdom “last forever.” What lesson does the article take from it?
options: Every power passes; yet each new holder of power imagines his own will last
Right. “Every flower withers and every house turns into ruins.”
Palaces ought to be built of stronger material
Not quite. The article says: Every power passes; yet each new holder of power imagines his own will last.
Stone inscriptions should be better preserved
Not quite. The article says: Every power passes; yet each new holder of power imagines his own will last.
Poets should not praise kings
Not quite. The article says: Every power passes; yet each new holder of power imagines his own will last.
questions.rationale: “Whenever someone achieves power on earth, he thinks that his power will last forever… But time has not supported this view of any ruler.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, are there disparities among people?
options: So that no one is self-sufficient and each completes himself by cooperating with others
Yes. Accepting this promotes cooperation and peace.
As a punishment
Not quite. The article says: So that no one is self-sufficient and each completes himself by cooperating with others.
So that some may look down on others
Not quite. The article says: So that no one is self-sufficient and each completes himself by cooperating with others.
By accident, with no purpose
Not quite. The article says: So that no one is self-sufficient and each completes himself by cooperating with others.
questions.rationale: “No individual is self-sufficient in this world. An individual completes himself only by associating with others.”

questions.article: Islam and the Myth of Two-Nation Theory
questions.q: Which example from the Prophet’s life does the article cite to show people of different faiths forming one civic community?
options: An order for other communities to leave
Not quite. The article says: The covenant of Madinah – “The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers,” each keeping its own religion.
A ban on dealings between communities
Not quite. The article says: The covenant of Madinah – “The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers,” each keeping its own religion.
The covenant of Madinah – “The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers,” each keeping its own religion
Exactly. Coexistence with mutual respect.
A treaty dividing the city into separate quarters
Not quite. The article says: The covenant of Madinah – “The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers,” each keeping its own religion.
questions.rationale: “The Jews of Banu Awf are one community with the believers. Jews have their religion, and Muslims have their religion.”

questions.q: What practical step does the answer on anger recommend when one feels angry?
options: Write an angry letter
Not quite. The article says: Keep silent – and sit down if standing – until the feeling subsides.
Leave home for a few days
Not quite. The article says: Keep silent – and sit down if standing – until the feeling subsides.
Keep silent – and sit down if standing – until the feeling subsides
Well read. Silence puts out the fire.
Speak at once so nothing is hidden
Not quite. The article says: Keep silent – and sit down if standing – until the feeling subsides.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet Muhammad advised that when one feels angry, they should either sit down if standing or remain quiet if speaking.”
